What stays unknown (read/mapfile/printf -v/+=, a loop over a substitution, $RANDOM, past source/eval, a substitution's value) keeps spec 204's D6.
decisions.why: This is the cure the last round asked for. Re-run in this reviewer's run through /tmp/t79/bin-r4 standing in the mirror, sid t and nobody: all five probes are refused or rewritten. So are last round's other forms that passed: cp /tmp/a $(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/f, echo x > $(echo /diagram)/f, touch $(basename /tmp/q/x), cd $(somewhere) && git commit. For what stays unknown, D6 is spec 204's conservative direction. The 29 bx rows pass, 29 of 29 for each sid (r4.b29.{t,nobody}.tsv, re-counted). The one form still passed, cp /tmp/a "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/f", is a quoted word holding a shell character, which is T83's class (ruled below). The other three passes are no write at all, as bash runs them: echo x > $UNSET/f, sed -i s/a/b/ $F and cp /tmp/a $DEST.

decisions.summary: A name nobody assigns takes its value in the guard's environment, else empty. So $UNSET/f is /f, and CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR is read as the project's directory although the Bash tool's shell leaves it unset.
decisions.why: This is where bash puts the write, as ruled last round. The premise is measured: the names only the Bash tool's shell sets (CLAUDE_JOB_DIR, CLAUDE_CODE_EXECPATH, CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS, the messaging socket, GIT_EDITOR, and others) are none of them a place in the mirror. That was re-read in this reviewer's shell. The recorded env-shell.txt holds names only, and a grep of it for /diagram is empty. The CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR misreading errs in the refusing direction, and the command it refuses writes /f, which is not good work. Not a defect.

decisions.summary: cd $UNSET is read as bash's cd with no word, that is $HOME, so cd $UNSET && git commit standing in the mirror is now allowed. Spec 204 FR-002 listed an unassigned variable as unresolvable, and its acceptance line names this exact command as not allowed silently.
decisions.why: This narrows spec 204 FR-002's letter, though constraint 2 calls FR-002 kept. D6's stated purpose is that the precision fix cannot become a bypass into main, and it does not here. In this reviewer's shell, bash -c 'cd /tmp; cd $UNSET && pwd' printed /home/agent, so the commit lands in $HOME, not in the mirror. The probe through bin-r4 is allowed, and HEAD refused it. The same yardstick passed $UNSET/f -> /f. The true unknown (cd $(somewhere)) stays refused and pinned. The block's cost paragraph discloses the change.

decisions.summary: git clone $R and git worktree add --detach $W, with R and W unset, are no write. git -C /x/$U commit is not in the mirror. Their unresolved pins move to $(cat url), $(cat w) and git -C <mirror>/$U.
decisions.why: Each pin moves to what bash and git do: a usage error with no tree made, or a place outside the mirror. The unresolved forms stay pinned under D6. Ruled the same way last round.

decisions.summary: Pins move in gm_tree_hooks, main_tree_hooks, readme_hooks (with its shell twins) and gate_write_hooks, plus main-tree fixture row 59 (rewrote -> allowed). Each keeps its old meaning through a form that stays unknown (read NAME, cd $(somewhere)).
decisions.why: A verdict changing as a bug is fixed is expected (fix as we go). Each moved pin either keeps its fail-closed meaning through a truly unknown form or moves to where bash writes.

decisions.summary: A name assigned more than once is judged at each of its values. D=/diagram/x; D=/tmp/y; touch $D/f standing in the mirror, a scratch write that HEAD passed, is now refused. The block lists this under 'its measured cost in full', not under Found and left.
decisions.why: It closes a real false allow (F=/diagram/a; echo x > $F; F=/tmp/b) and judges if/else branches both ways, which is good. But the refusal it leaves is a wrong outcome, a check refusing good work (constitution XIV v2.36.0). It contradicts the block's own goal 1, 'no scratch write refused because a variable stands in its name'. It is newly introduced: HEAD allowed it and bin-r4 refuses it (p1.r4.tsv row 22, re-run). It is not impossible to avoid, because the command's text shows a straight-line reassignment with no branch between. Last round held that 'none in the corpus' counts how often a wrong verdict happens, not whether it is wrong, and the same standard applies here. The refusing direction makes it cheaper, but not exempt from FR-009. The cure needs no code: carry it as a Found and left item with why it is not fixed here, a filed task id and its order (FR-009). Fixing it in T79 is the other cure.

decisions.summary: The walk binds a many-valued name up to 64 values. Past that, it falls back. The block does not say to what, and the cost paragraph does not list it.
decisions.why: Measured in this reviewer's run through bin-r4 and bin-head, standing in the mirror, sid nobody, main-tree alone and all guards. A loop over 65 or 70 literal scratch values (for f in /tmp/q/1 ... /tmp/q/70; do touch $f; done) is refused by bin-r4 and allowed by HEAD. 63 values pass. So past the cap the name falls to D6. That keeps the mirror safe (a mirror value in position 1 or 70 is refused, as is a nested '.' value), but it refuses scratch work HEAD passed. The block calls its cost paragraph 'its measured cost in full', and it does not list this. The 'what stays unknown' list does not name the cap either. Bounding the work is a fair design, but the wrong outcome it leaves must be stated and either fixed (judge a single name's values linearly, for example) or carried as a Found and left item with why, a filed id and its order (FR-009). The block must also name the cap's fallback.

decisions.summary: A quoted word holding a space or a shell character is blanked, so the destination is misread. cp /tmp/a "/diagram/x y" passes, and so does cp /tmp/a "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/f" (re-probed). Left as T83, to land before T22.
decisions.why: This is a pre-existing defect. The why is concrete: the blanking keeps commit messages, sed scripts and programs from being read as paths by every guard, so a fix needs its own corpus replay. It is filed with an id and an order (FR-009).

decisions.summary: make-only refuses a guard file's name (Makefile, dev/work-budget.json, a guard's source) written into a $(mktemp -d) place or a scratch copy in a loop's body (12 replay moves). Left as T87, to land before T22.
decisions.why: HEAD refuses the same write to a literal scratch path. The rule is the guard-file list's, read by layer 3 and make-only alike, outside the walk. It carries why, a filed id and an order.

decisions.summary: A python3 -c program that writes a place it computes from sys.argv is judged where the shell stands. Now that loop bodies are seen, three corpus scratch writes are newly refused (bx#54240, bx#58694, ux#2209). Left as T89, to land before T22.
decisions.why: HEAD refuses the same program outside a loop. These three refusals come from fixing a false allow (unseen loop bodies), and keeping that false allow would be the worse defect. The rule is py_c's, outside the walk, and needs its own replay. It carries why, a filed id and an order.

decisions.summary: gate-write reads a target's command from a segment cut at 120 characters. A make behind long VAR=value prefixes, in a loop's body, is newly refused (ux#1371). Left as T90, to land before T22.
decisions.why: HEAD refuses the same line outside a loop. The why is concrete: readme_hooks' kept-segment rule reads the cut, so the fix is a field of its own on the target. It carries why, a filed id and an order.

decisions.summary: readme_hooks.rs substitutes $(mktemp) itself, as the walk now does. Not filed.
decisions.why: The two agree, so there is no wrong outcome. A difference that works is not a defect.

decisions.summary: house-style's /tmp/ 'outside' prefix makes three replay moves an artifact of a mirror under /tmp. On their real paths, a direct run shows both binaries correcting them.
decisions.why: A limit of the measurement, named so the moves are read correctly. Not a defect of the guard.

decisions.summary: The run's starter is read from its output path's task id and the event log's PostToolUse launch line (bg = id, by = the payload's agent_id), not from the env
decisions.why: The brief's constraint: the starter from the run's process (its env or the event log's launch line), not a guess; item 4 measured that the env carries no agent id, so the launch line is the one source that can name it.

decisions.summary: A launch line with no by is the session's own background call, the harness's to wake, permitted
decisions.why: Feature 246's design as the brief states it: a run the harness tracks is let through. The 10 rows of the 24 are this case.

decisions.summary: A by still running by set_down_hooks' transcript reading (T65's) is the builder's, permitted with one line (builder-running)
decisions.why: The task's own finding: 14 of the 24 refusals named a run a still-running builder had started.

decisions.summary: Any other by - stopped, or the transcript cannot say - is judged as a detached run: watched by a waiter or refused once per root
decisions.why: Keeps the refusal the brief requires (still fire for a stopped builder's run) and takes the safe side where the starter's state cannot be read, as 'not a guess' asks.

decisions.summary: A run no launch line names is a call an agent is still in, and stays the harness's
decisions.why: Measured 2026-11-20 23:22:49 (item 4): a background call's PostToolUse can arrive after the Stop. Items 1 and 12 state that a detached unwatched run and a stopped builder's run still refuse once per root, so the block does not let the main session's own detached run through; whether the code holds that is the tests' and the code review's job, not fidelity's.

decisions.summary: A new read-only set_down_hooks::still_running(path, id); running() and its verdict left as T65 left them
decisions.why: The brief names one public reader added to set_down_hooks, read-only, and running() unchanged; item 4 measured why running() alone misses interim builders (11 of 14).

decisions.summary: The Stop payload's background_tasks subagent list is not the reading used
decisions.why: Measured 2026-11-21 (item 4): every builder missing from a Stop's list had last sent an interim notice, so the list cannot say a builder is waiting on its own run. A choice of source inside the task.

decisions.summary: Procs::harness takes comm or argv[0]'s first word 'claude', so a version-named harness of a background session is the harness
decisions.why: A check refusing good work (the 10 rows), a defect found on the way and fixed in this task, as the project's fix-what-you-find rule asks; measured (6 harness processes, 4 version-named).

decisions.summary: The heading restates the finding by its measurement: 14 builder-started runs and 10 the session's own background call's run
decisions.why: The restatement widens the fix to the 10 rows the measurement found and drops nothing; no row is a stopped builder's. The filed T85 line itself is not in the bundle, so this is judged on the restatement as given.

decisions.summary: A run started by a builder's own sub-agent (an id the session's transcript never names) still reads as stopped and refuses, as before
decisions.why: Neither the request nor FR-013 says what this guard must cover, so this leaves nothing asked undone; and no wrong outcome is measured - none in the 24 rows, and the wider window's 34 (19, 14, 1 both) leave none unaccounted for. The default is the guard's safe side for a starter whose state cannot be read. Not a defect left, so FR-009's deferral form is not owed.

decisions.summary: The caller's files are the clone's uncommitted files less those that another task's non-fallback Edit/Write/NotebookEdit event-log lines alone name (newer than the file's last commit, inside a 7-day window); an unnamed file and a shared file are the caller's; the feature comes from F= or the latest task-start naming the task.
decisions.why: This is how the task's own fix is built (a closing run judges the caller's work, the [perf] builders' loop under FR-013). It errs to the safe side: a miss counts a file as the caller's and gives a false red, never a false green. Choosing it over the active-task mark and over a FILES=/CRATES= list is a design choice, and the plan measured all three.

decisions.summary: A new GUESS knob: an edit line claims a file only if it is newer than the file's last commit, within 7 days.
decisions.why: A parameter of the mechanism. When it misjudges, it counts more files as the caller's, so it can only make the verdict stricter.

decisions.summary: In static's per-crate steps, a red crate whose kept-key inputs read none of the caller's files is reported APART and not counted. The key inputs are factored out of verdict_key_with so the two cannot drift. A crate that builds on a caller's crate, or whose tests read the caller's file, is the caller's. A listing or key that cannot be judged counts every crate.
decisions.why: This is the fix the task's line asks for (shape (a), 5 runs measured). Every case that cannot be judged falls back to counting, as before.

decisions.summary: Tree-wide steps and hooks-test stay counted whole, and a crate holding both tasks' files is judged whole (shapes (d) and (e), 4 of the 13 measured runs, stay red).
decisions.why: This narrows the task's aim of a verdict on the caller's own work, but separating these cases is impossible with the instrument the plan has. Every hooks-test suite's key reads 994-998 paths of the guard's and the gate's crates (measured with l7r-guard deps), so a suite run on another task's edit also ran the caller's code, and no key can clear it. A crate's lint and cover verdict is one verdict over the whole crate. The tree-wide steps, measured through quick's full runs, fired on no other task's file. A red that is kept is not a wrong green, and none of these cases is a check refusing work that could be shown good.

decisions.summary: A counted red whose every error line names another task's file (the caller's crate or the gate binary unbuildable on another task's half-done dependency) is tagged BLOCKED, names the files and tasks, and stays red.
decisions.why: Nothing of the caller's was judged there, so keeping it red is correct. The tag only reports which task is responsible.

decisions.summary: With no T= the whole clone is judged as before. Only the script sets the listing, so make static, make done and a landing judge every crate by construction.
decisions.why: Keeps the landing's whole-tree check and the default unchanged. Nothing is narrowed.

decisions.summary: T55's decide notice and foreground refusal (order.rs) and the third-static refusal (static_runs_hooks.rs) now name 'make closing-checks T=<task> F=<feature>' from the call's filed task, or T=<your task> when the call is filed under no task. closing-checks.sh's rerun line names T= and F= as given.
decisions.why: Without this the fix cannot be reached: a builder told to run a bare make closing-checks gets the whole-clone verdict that T86 exists to replace. Fixing the third-static message beside the other two is the same defect (constitution XIV), and its red-first tests are recorded.

decisions.summary: Files another builder writes through Bash (sed -i, heredoc, generator) leave no Edit/Write line, so they count as the caller's. This is left to T93 (a write-path field on the event log's Bash lines in rust/guard/shared's event_log_hooks), which lands before T22.
decisions.why: A defect, a false red on good work, is left out of T86, but it is not dropped. FR-009's deferral form is met in full: why it is not fixed here (a new field on the event log's Bash lines that every reader of the log meets, in another crate's files), the filed id T93, its order 'lands before T22', and an every-instance line labeled observed 2026-11-21 with its method. The GM approved 'briefs that default to fixing in the task' (improvement 4), which allows a deferral that states why. The miss is on the safe side (never a wrong green, and make done judges the whole tree). It does not gut T86's purpose: the 5 measured shape-(a) runs all came apart under the replayed rule.

decisions.id: T84-1 task-add lock and own withdrawal
decisions.summary: make task-add takes a per-feature flock held from the id's read through both quick runs, withdraws only its own box and section from the files as they are; past a 120 s wait (GUESS, knob L7R_TASK_ADD_LOCK_WAIT) it refuses, writing nothing and naming the lock file.
decisions.why: The brief asks to measure first and lock red first if two filings collide; item 4 measured 6 of 6 rounds losing both filings on a red quick, and item 9 shows red then green. It keeps FR-011's withdraw-and-refuse behavior and only stops it taking another writer's lines. A lock-wait timeout that refuses fails closed.

decisions.id: T84-2 nothing built for a builder's own review
decisions.summary: No new code lets a builder dispatch its own spec-fidelity review: measured, every builder dispatch already passes every guard; only the briefs barred it.
decisions.why: The finding's cause is that instructions alone barred it; the measurement (35 calls, none refused) shows no guard stands in the way. That the review actually happens is enforced by T84-3's stop guard and the tick gate (T84-4), so this is not enforcement by instruction.

decisions.id: T84-3a builder-stop guard: who is held
decisions.summary: builder_stop_hooks (SubagentStop) answers decision: block to a builder the session dispatched for a started, open task while l7r-gate plan decided says its section is not decided (the verdict store's current CLEAR, plus the decide lint's deferral findings).
decisions.why: The brief names SubagentStop and reading the verdict store rather than text; builder identity follows D8. A builder with no started task is not held here, but the tick and push gate still refuse its task's landing without a CLEAR section, so no unreviewed work lands through that gap.

decisions.summary: A builder past T12's context cap, in its handoff-only state, may stop.
decisions.why: The brief requires it (the context cap's handoff-only state passing), and FR-006 sends that builder to a handoff and a fresh dispatch; the next builder is held by the same guard and the tick gate stays the backstop.

decisions.summary: The stop guard has an escape of a recorded reason.
decisions.why: The brief and the project's guard rules (FR-012's form) require it. Approach item 3 does not spell the escape out; item 2 lists it as a constraint and the suite pins the guard (6 passed).

decisions.summary: The guard's call to the gate is limited to 40 s (GUESS, under the hook's 60 s).
decisions.why: A new constant, labeled a GUESS. The section does not say which way a timeout goes (block or let the builder stop). Either way the tick and push gate (T84-4) still refuse an undecided section, so a timed-out ask cannot land unreviewed work. Noted, not blocking.

decisions.id: T84-4a plan gate per task: an open task's section not judged
decisions.summary: The tick's and the push's plan gate (plan::tick_gate, task::push_owed) judges the blocks outside every task's section plus the sections of the task ticked and the tasks ticked before it, and never an open task's section; the land crate keeps no plan check of its own.
decisions.why: This narrows feature 243 / 375 D60's reach (every block owed) at the tick and push. Applying the whole-feature rule literally defeats its own purpose and the GM's 'real enforcement and not just instructions': measured, all 16 of 451's landings took PLAN_REVIEW_OK, 10 of them on correct work, so the gate had become a routine escape. 243's purpose is that a task is not ticked while its decisions lack a verdict. That holds: the ticked task's own section, earlier ticked sections and every shared block are still judged, and an open task's section is judged at its own tick. No task can be ticked or pushed while its own section lacks CLEAR at its digest. The red test a_tick_answers_for_its_own_section_the_ticked_ones_and_the_shared_blocks pins it.

decisions.id: T84-4b a filled template's old heading not owed
decisions.summary: A '(removed) ### T<n> (<why: ...>)' block, the old heading of a filled task template, is not owed once T<n>'s section carries a CLEAR task verdict.
decisions.why: Adjudicated apart from 4a. D60 owes a deleted block because a decision deleted by hand is a change. A template's placeholder heading carries no decision: the text replacing it is the task's own section, already reviewed CLEAR at its digest. Measured: 4 of 16 landings owed only this. This holds only as far as the forgiveness is limited to the template's placeholder heading of the same task with a current CLEAR section, as the section states. A hand-deleted decision under any other heading stays owed.

decisions.id: T84-5 left: arbiter accept not recorded as a task verdict (T92)
decisions.summary: A round-arbiter accept is not written to the verdict store as the task's verdict; T33, T46, T67 and T79 show BLOCKED there. Left to T92's line, lands before T22.
decisions.why: A defect that refuses correct work, left in the FR-009 form: its visible effect, measured 2026-11-21, why it is not fixed here (the accept is written by make arbiter-ruled, outside this task's files), filed id T92, and 'lands before T22'. That is the form the four accepts in rulings.md treat as enough. One gap for T92 to cover: the new stop guard reads the same store, so a builder of a task the arbiter accepted would also be held at its stop, not only its tick and push. Same defect, same cure, and an escape exists.

decisions.id: T84-6 left: land crate tests take the session's PLAN_REVIEW_OK (T94)
decisions.summary: The land crate's tests read the session's exported escape and write the real guard log; filed as T94, lands before T22.
decisions.why: A defect (a test's verdict follows the session's exports, and make audit lists a fixture's escape as real) left in FR-009's form: the observation and its method, why (the land crate's tests are outside this task's files, and T84 makes the escape rare rather than gone), filed id T94, and its order.

decisions.id: T84-7 printf recipe lines: not a defect
decisions.summary: task_add/quick.rs's lines() drops any quick recipe line opening printf; today no check opens so.
decisions.why: Measured against the Makefile: no check is skipped, so nothing goes wrong. Under constitution XIV this is a difference, not a defect, and needs no ruling.

decisions.summary: The write targets are logged on a Bash call's END lines (PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure), not its start; the start was priced and not taken, and the failure end is included.
decisions.why: This is how T93's line gets done, and it is the more conservative choice: a refused call whose start would have claimed the caller's own file for another task would give a wrong green. It narrows nothing in the GM's request or the accepted spec.

decisions.summary: writes leaves out programs that only read, targets the walk cannot place, and directories; no target means no field; the form is pinned.
decisions.why: A file that no line names stays the caller's, so an exclusion can only cost a saving, never give a wrong green. This choice is about precision, and it takes away nothing that was asked for. The Python-heredoc gap it creates is ruled on separately, as T93-python-heredoc-left.

decisions.summary: No walk is reused or memoized, because no guard walks at PostToolUse (each hook event runs in its own process, observed with a method). A memo in shared::tree is not added.
decisions.why: The brief asked for reuse only where the process had already done the walk. The plan measured that this never happens, so the condition never holds and nothing asked for is dropped.

decisions.summary: closing-checks.sh claims a dirty file only by an exact edit path or writes path, never by a prefix, under T86's existing rules (no fallback line, a task named, newer than the last commit, never the caller's). The header's list of what stays the caller's is restated.
decisions.why: This is the reader half of the task's own goal. The exact-path rule stops a make at the clone root from claiming the whole clone for another task, which would be a wrong green.

decisions.summary: A log line older than its own task's last 'ticked (make land)' commit claims nothing. This fixes a T86 defect found during T93's own closing run (T66's stale Edit line on rust/guard/CLAUDE.md).
decisions.why: A defect found in the work is fixed in the task (fix as we go, constitution XIV). It is a wrong outcome (a caller's own red reported apart, a wrong green), it lives in a file the task already owns, and the red-first test is recorded.

decisions.summary: A prefilter that would skip 35.5% of commands was measured and not taken: it would lose 6 files and add a second list of writers that could drift from the walk.
decisions.why: This is a design choice inside the task, and it keeps the full coverage the task asks for.

decisions.summary: writes keeps /tmp paths and is not cut to the clone's paths (1.56% log growth, measured).
decisions.why: A choice of form with a measured cost. It narrows nothing asked for.

decisions.summary: The first walk in a process costs 3.2-8.6 ms (about 3.89 ms added per Bash end, roughly 37 s a night). It is left in place, called not a defect, and proposed as a [perf] task of its own in shared::tree.
decisions.why: Every verdict and every line stays right, only slower, so under constitution XIV (v2.36.0) this is not a defect and needs no ruling. The cost is measured and stated, and it is passed on as a performance task rather than hidden.

decisions.summary: Files written by a Python program run from a heredoc or -c get no writes entry: the walk places them where the shell stands. The reader for them, program_names, is in the guard crate, which the shared event log cannot reach. Filed as T96, to land before T22. Measured effect: T86's runs 2 and 3 stay red on the task and plan crates, and 15 of the night's 51 still-missed files.
decisions.why: T93's own line covers 'shell-written files', and these are shell-written, so leaving them narrows the task as filed. The defect is not dropped and not carried past the next step. It is filed as T96, with its reason and its order ('lands before T22', T86's filing) as FR-009 requires, and every instance was measured and classed. The reason is concrete: shared cannot depend on the guard crate, so the reader for these programs lives outside T93's files. Splitting the fix this way does not undermine the request's purpose (performance work first, closing verdicts that are not red on another builder's files), because T93's part removes wrong reds now and introduces no wrong green.

decisions.summary: T93 is ordered as a [perf] task under FR-013 (the builders' loop), with no engine performance checklist.
decisions.why: The GM asked on 2026-11-21 that the closing-checks work be filed as a performance task, and FR-013 counts the builders' loop as performance work. T93 extends that work.

decisions.summary: Replace the million-step spelling test's 20 s wall-clock bound with a bound on the search thread's own CPU time (read from /proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/schedstat every 100 ms), CPU_BOUND_NS = 30 s, a CONVENTION and a knob; a panicked thread fails at once.
decisions.why: The test refuses good work under load (measured: 6 named reds at load ~82, 33 of 88 red on the loaded reproduction) - a check that refuses correct work is a defect (constitution XIV) and fixing known defects is the GM's standing rule; the bound still serves T185's stated purpose (a spin fails rather than hangs), shown by mutant M2 failing at 30 s CPU, and honors 'time is never a gate'. Nothing the GM asked for is narrowed.

decisions.summary: Pin the test's premise by the limit firing: a build of the house style pattern with fancy_regex's old 1,000,000-step limit must err on the test text.
decisions.why: Enforcement of what the test exists to catch (the step limit regression, mutant M1); it adds no behavior and only fails when the thing it guards is absent.

decisions.summary: Scope: the test file alone - no engine code, no guard code, T88's and T93's files untouched.
decisions.why: Confines the fix to the defect; narrows nothing the request or spec asked for.

decisions.summary: Found and left: eight other test files carrying the same 20 s wall bound, not filed, because none has failed by it outside T185's own red-first run (measured census).
decisions.why: Per constitution XIV a defect is a wrong outcome; no wrong outcome was measured for these eight, so leaving them is not deferring a defect and FR-009's filed-task requirement does not reach them.

decisions.summary: Classed as performance work ([perf]) under FR-013: a sound scan no longer failing a crate's tests under load keeps builders from re-running and chasing reds not theirs.
decisions.why: FR-013 counts work that makes 'the builders' loop faster' as performance work, carrying the GM's 2026-11-20 'prioritize performance improvements going forward'; spurious reds cost builder re-runs, so the class fits.

decisions.summary: T81 lands once T88's coverage is green (closing-checks red only on T88's files, none of T81's lines named).
decisions.why: Ordering of landings; it narrows nothing asked.

decisions.summary: With other work uncommitted in the clone, make land runs whole in a persistent landing worktree <clone>-land at the clone's HEAD, under a lock, seeded with the clone's kept results; the clone then takes the landed tip (update-ref, merge-tree/commit-tree, three-way merge-file, conflict moves nothing, exit 4).
decisions.why: A design for a [perf] task under FR-013 (the landings). It narrows nothing the GM asked: the gate still judges the tree pushed, the push's dirty-tree refusal and the stamp's disk key are unchanged, and the two other ways are measured and rejected on their costs.

decisions.summary: The landing refuses the landing tasks' own edits still uncommitted (PostToolUse edit lines under the task naming a dirty file newer than its last commit), naming the git commit command; dirty files no task's edit names stay in the clone, not landed.
decisions.why: Keeps the landed tree the task's own work; no requested behavior is narrowed. Red-first pair recorded (78/3 then 81).

decisions.summary: While something runs, the Stop hook refuses a stop when fewer than L7R_BUILDERS (GUESS 3) builders run and next_independent names an open task never started, after no open task, touching no running task's named files; escape is make set-down F= WHY=.
decisions.why: Adds a refusal in service of the builders' loop; it carries a reasoned, recorded escape and a named compliant command, and red-first is recorded (350/2 then 352). Narrows nothing asked.

decisions.summary: next_independent takes performance work first across every active feature, then the rest, feature-first then each active feature by its last task-start.
decisions.why: This is FR-013's own clause: the Stop hook's start-the-next names an open performance task before any other, across active features. The plan corrected an earlier feature-first ordering that broke it (r1 red, r2 green).

decisions.summary: Where the task the Stop hook names is not performance work, its named make task-start carries PERF_LATER_OK - which happens only when every open performance task is started, waits on an open task, or overlaps a running task's files.
decisions.why: This narrows how far FR-013's task-start refusal reaches in practice, so it is ruled. It uses FR-013's own escape, of a reason, recorded, for the case that escape names: a performance task that cannot start now because it waits on another task's landing (or is already running). The hook names a non-perf task only after no performance task can be started. Leaving slots empty in that case would not get performance work done any sooner, and would undo the GM's purpose ('doing those first makes everything after them faster'), which is ordering, not idling. Each start still needs the escape typed in and logged.

decisions.summary: Overlap is read from a task line's named files or *_hooks modules against running tasks' edit lines, with specs/, .git/ and the ledger excluded and common basenames matched only with a path; a line naming nothing fails toward a start.
decisions.why: A design detail of the dispatch rule; its stated cost (two builders in one crate) is judged by T86's closing checks. Narrows nothing asked.

decisions.summary: L7R_BUILDERS is a new knob, GUESS 3, labeled at its point of change (set_down_hooks.rs BUILDERS); D14's knob table row is T22's.
decisions.why: D14 asks for a GUESS label at the point of change, and T88 gives one. The knob table is a task the spec assigns elsewhere, so this sets no new rule. T22 has to list this knob when it builds the table.

decisions.summary: 449 T244's stop before the parked homestead stages is not built here; 444 is set down, so free_slot names no 444 stage task now, and a stop there passes by make set-down naming the GM's ruling.
decisions.why: The rolling-dispatch refusal does not force work the GM ruled to stop before: 444 is set down (measured from set-downs.jsonl and task-starts.jsonl), and the escape the refusal names takes his ruling as its WHY. T244 belongs to 449.

decisions.summary: The landing worktree's own target (13 GB measured) is not pruned whole; only the sweep's per-crate variant rule trims it, and a hand-deleted clone leaves its -land until the directory goes.
decisions.why: A stated cost, not a wrong outcome; nothing the GM asked is narrowed.

decisions.summary: The after-occupancy measurement is filed as T98, lands before T22, because it needs a night of rolling dispatch first.
decisions.why: It cannot be measured before a night runs on the change. It is filed with an order, as FR-009 requires, and the before-figure uses the replay's method, so before and after are measured one way.

decisions.summary: test-idle-tests-hooks.sh's wall-clock case refused good work under load (red at load 16.5, green on rerun); filed as T99, lands before T22, as another guard's suite outside T88's files.
decisions.why: A defect, but T88 is not the one carrying it forward. It is filed with its reason, its id and its order, which is what FR-009 asks of a deferral. FIX AS WE GO's rule about steps applies to 449's port, and this defect is still put ahead of T22. The GM did not ask T88 to fix this suite.

decisions.summary: blocked() reads cover's '<path> - lines no test reaches: <lines>' lines (path stripped to the clone's, first line a real one) beside the '-->' and 'Diff in' paths; a coverage red whose every named file is another task's is tagged BLOCKED naming each file and task.
decisions.why: This is the defect T95's line names (a coverage red on another's files went untagged) fixed as found, in the closing checks the GM had filed as a performance task (2026-11-21). It adds no behavior beyond making T86's tag read the coverage output it missed.

decisions.summary: A BLOCKED red stays counted red; 'red' and the exit are untouched.
decisions.why: Keeps T86's rule as it was. The tag only informs the builder and blocks or passes nothing new.

decisions.summary: The tag's wording says which lines it read: errors only keep T86's words, uncovered lines only say 'yours are covered ... re-run once their tests reach them', both say 'nothing of yours failed there'.
decisions.why: Message wording that comes with D1. It neither narrows nor adds scope.

decisions.summary: A failed coverage run's marker '<crate> - lines no test reaches: 0' is not read as a path.
decisions.why: The marker names a crate, not a file. Reading it as a path would wrongly untag a run whose cover build broke on another task's file (the 12:47Z run, measured). Leaving it out keeps D1 correct, and the run is still tagged from its '-->' errors (red-first case: BLOCKED).

decisions.summary: An APART crate's block (its 'rust-checks: APART' header up to the next 'rust-checks:' line) is not read, so another task's APART lines no longer tag a caller's own red BLOCKED. The caller's own uncovered line beside another's error is also no longer tagged.
decisions.why: Two wrong-tag defects in the same function, found while building it and fixed here. The project's fix-as-we-go rule covers this, and it is not unrequested scope. Each is pinned by a red-first suite case.

decisions.summary: T81's run (the run cited in T95's line) stays untagged after the fix. Two of its three uncovered files were named by no task's event line before the run, so T86's rule counts them as the caller's. Naming them is left to the split's tasks T93 (Bash writes) and T96 (a Python program's writes).
decisions.why: The defect T95's line names (blocked() not reading cover's lines) is fully fixed, and the replay shows the fixed function tags T84's 17:10Z coverage-only red, which HEAD did not. T81's run stays untagged because of a different, already-filed defect: which files the split attributes to which task. Under T86's rule an unattributed file is the caller's, so the result is a missing tag, never a wrong one. Neither the GM's request nor the spec asks T95 to change attribution, so nothing is narrowed. The plan states T81's run is not tagged and does not overclaim it.

decisions.summary: Red-first suite cases (46 passed, 3 failed against the unfixed function; 49 of 49 fixed) and the task's own closing run as the exits. Other tasks' files (T93, T88, T97, T82) are not touched.
decisions.why: Verification of what the task fixes, plus scope discipline. Both are within.

decisions.summary: T95 is not classed as performance work (no [perf]).
decisions.why: The task changes what a tag reads, not how long a run takes. Under FR-013 the class only sets scheduling order. It does not narrow what the GM asked for or what the spec requires.

decisions.summary: requirements gains a third pass (ANY_ITEM) reading a dashless bold FR/SC id, carried from its start to the next requirement of any form or the next heading
decisions.why: This is T82's own line: the reader answered NOT FOUND for requirement text that exists, a tool answering wrongly (a defect under XIV). Measured on the real 449 and 383 bundles; red-first tests named.

decisions.summary: the same pass also reads an indented sub-item with its own id (184's and 295's FR-005a..d), carried as a list item; labeled deliberate addition
decisions.why: It widens the fix and does not narrow it. The task's own bundle showed the same wrong outcome (NOT FOUND for existing text) in the same reader, and fixing known defects in the task is the GM's standing rule (fix as we go). The differential shows 0 of 4,751 existing reads changing, so nothing asked for is given up.

decisions.summary: an id a list item or heading already gives keeps that text; a dashless restatement of it is commentary and is not read over it
decisions.why: This keeps every existing correct read unchanged (the brief's constraint) and does not cut anything T82 asked for. The dashless ids T82 targets (287 in 21 specs) have no other form.

decisions.summary: spec_amendments keeps ITEM rather than sharing the new pattern
decisions.why: Measured: no spec writes a dashless id under an Amendment heading, so no wrong outcome exists there today. T82's line and brief name the requirement reader alone. A difference with no defect is not one that needs fixing.

decisions.summary: indented bold ids with no dash (192's, 198's) and a bare id opening a line are not read as requirement definitions
decisions.why: Measured as commentary on ids defined elsewhere, so not reading them leaves no requirement NOT FOUND. Nothing T82 asks for is excluded.

decisions.summary: exits and done: plan crate tests, lint, format, 100% cover, before/after bundles differing in the NOT FOUND line alone, closing-checks green; order before T22
decisions.why: This is enforcement and verification of the requested fix and of T48's ordering. It adds no behavior beyond the fix.

decisions.summary: Every walk static (40 in tree.rs, tree/bind.rs, tree/python.rs, tree/py_c.rs) becomes shared::regex::Lazy: built on first use as before, searched only where a necessary literal of the pattern stands in the text, else no match and nothing built.
decisions.why: This is the [perf] task T97's line files under FR-013 (the builders' loop, every Bash call's hooks), and the GM asked that performance work go first (request.md 2026-11-20). The plan states each gate is a literal every match holds; its replay of 9,646 commands shows the guards' verdicts unchanged, so the hooks still do their job. It removes work and narrows nothing that was asked.

decisions.summary: is_match/captures read a search error as no match, as every call site already did; captures_iter/find_iter keep yielding Result items so each of their 12 call sites keeps .map_while(Result::ok).
decisions.why: This keeps the existing handling and the checks crate's regex_scans rule. It is an implementation detail inside the task and narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: Five patterns that need no literal (CHMOD_MODE, py_c's WRITES, READ_MODE, ANY_MODE, EXPANDS) get a gate that passes every text.
decisions.why: These are unchanged behavior where no gate is sound. Nothing is narrowed.

decisions.summary: PLAIN_QUOTE_BODY is replaced by plain code (plain_quote_body), with char::is_whitespace standing for \s, pinned by a differential test over every character to U+3100 plus U+180E, U+200B, U+FEFF.
decisions.why: It does the same job faster, and the differential test enforces that the answers agree. That serves the performance request.

decisions.summary: py_c's REPLACE (the literal replace\() becomes contains("replace(").
decisions.why: A literal pattern is turned into a literal search with the same meaning, faster. Within the perf task.

decisions.summary: A hand-written scan for ASSIGN's shape is not taken. About 12.4% of commands (an estimate, measured 2026-11-21) still build ASSIGN when they hold an = that is not an assignment.
decisions.why: Judged against request.md, FR-013 and this section's own statement of T97's line, since the line itself is not in the bundle. None of them sets a target for this task. Leaving a further speedup untaken is a design choice, not a defect (constitution XIV: only slower, every answer right). The task's purpose is still met: from a median of 12 builds a command to 2.

decisions.summary: A child-process pin test prints the patterns its process built (regex::BUILT, a list kept in test builds alone): simple commands build none, and a redirect builds exactly REDIRECT.
decisions.why: This is a test that fails only when the requested speedup is absent. Under FR-012 it is enforcement of the request, not unrequested scope.

decisions.summary: Fix a race in tests/hooks/test-no-poll-hooks.sh, outside T97's files, that turned its closing run 2 red. The case now ages the quiet file again first.
decisions.why: A flaky test that refuses good work is a defect under XIV. Fix-as-we-go asks known defects to be fixed as found, and this widens no requested behavior.

decisions.summary: The closing checks are not run a fourth time. Run 3's static was red at its format step on T100's in-flight file before reaching any T97 crate; T97's crates are shown green by crate-scoped test, lint and cover after the last edit.
decisions.why: No requirement in spec-index or request.md asks a task for a green closing run. FR-007 and improvement 2 point the other way: they cap make static at two, with crate-scoped checks while iterating and make static once at the end, which the landing's gate supplies. Run 3 was already a recorded STATIC_OK escape. This does depart from the plan's own exit in item 6 (a green make closing-checks), and the caller should square that line with item 9. It is not a narrowing of what the GM asked.

decisions.summary: shape's strip_heredocs and strip_quotes stay ungated: they are outside T97's files and are proposed as a separate [perf] task, not fixed here.
decisions.why: FR-009 bites only on a deferred DEFECT. This is not one: every answer is right and only slower (XIV, the GM 2026-11-19 definition), so leaving it unchanged stays within scope. Aside: no task id is filed for it yet, and under FR-013's ordering the caller may wish to file it.

decisions.summary: The saving over the dispatcher's whole event (about 2.7 ms at a Bash start) is left an estimate. A replay through every guard would write real guard state in a shared clone.
decisions.why: It is labeled an estimate and its arithmetic reconciles (3.23 - 0.21 - 0.30). It decides no scope: the per-guard saving is measured, and the estimate only reports what the task gains.

decisions.summary: T97 is classed as performance work ([perf], FR-013: the builders' loop).
decisions.why: It speeds every Bash call's hooks, which is within FR-013's 'the builders' loop'.

decisions.summary: The active-task mark stays one object (the last task started); only the hold changes; task-start's append and the event log's filing are untouched.
decisions.why: Leaves every other reader of the mark (measured search) as it is; the change is confined to the refusal the task was filed against.

decisions.summary: Where the mark's open task holds, a landing lands beside it when each of its tasks is started in the clone, its section passes `plan decided`, and no file of its delta (sectioned files and review ledger aside) carries an edit or shell write filed under another OPEN task since the file last landed; each failing reason is named with the hold.
decisions.why: This is the fix the filed task asks for (a ready, CLEAR, closing-checked task refused 'held by' a task started after it). 405 D4's purpose - no push of the worked task's half-done work - is kept as the files-its-own test, so the rule's purpose is not gutted; the mark's task is now protected the way every other started task beside it already was (D4: no other open box holds).

decisions.summary: A ready ruling exports L7R_LAND_READY; holding_with holds nothing for the ticks it names, so the push and the CI merge read the landing's own ruling; where the first pass did not rule, the push's step asks again (export_ready); the ruling never reads which task the mark names.
decisions.why: Measured that a first-pass-only fix lands nothing (the push re-asks the hold); carrying one ruling to all three askers is what makes the fix reach its stated case.

decisions.summary: The hold's one condition is edited in shared::speckit (holding_with) under make guard-edit, a labeled deviation from the launcher's file list; T97's shared/src/tree* and T82's files untouched.
decisions.why: The launcher's file list is not the GM's words; the edit sits where the rule actually lives (one rule, three callers) and touches no other open task's files. Implementation placement is not a fidelity question.

decisions.summary: Padding L7R_LAND_TICKS with the mark's task, and a new `l7r-gate land --held` verb, priced and not taken.
decisions.why: Design alternatives declined for stated correctness reasons (a padded TICKS would name a task the landing does not tick); nothing asked is dropped.

decisions.summary: land-alone step 2, under its lock taken first, commits plan.md, tasks.md and plan-review.json built from HEAD with only the landing tasks' pieces replaced (temporary index, commit-tree, compare-and-swap update-ref), working files untouched; step 3's own-files refusal passes over the sectioned files.
decisions.why: Implements the task's second half (T95, CLEAR, could not land alone because plan.md also held T82's and T97's unreviewed sections); dry run on the real T95 case measured the commit carrying only T95's pieces.

decisions.summary: The staging lives in scripts/land-alone.sh's Python (PYLIB), not the land crate, so one program holds the pieces' rule for staging and take-back.
decisions.why: Placement choice; no part of the request reaches it.

decisions.summary: Where git merge-file conflicts on a sectioned file at take-back (measured shape: a tick's archive meeting another task's edit of the next heading), the file is merged piece by piece; a piece both sides changed differently still conflicts and nothing moves, as before.
decisions.why: Needed for (2) to work on the shape measured; keeps the existing stop on a true conflict.

decisions.summary: The files-own test does not see a file written by a Python program (the event log names no file for it; T96, open) and takes an edit older than 7 days as landed (land-alone's existing LANDED_SINCE bound).
decisions.why: Adjudicated each part. Python writes: the file name is absent from the log until T96 lands, so the test cannot see it; the gap already governs every started task other than the mark's under 405 D4 and land-alone's existing own-files refusal, so T101 adds no new class of exposure, and the fix is an already-filed open task (T96). 7-day bound: it is land-alone's own existing bound, reused rather than introduced. Neither removes anything the GM asked for in 451, and neither guts D4's purpose for the work the log does attribute.

decisions.summary: Case 5's clock seam holds the timer's first reading behind a gate file. The first jump is written only once that reading is taken, so it lands inside the wait by a condition and not by the shell's timing.
decisions.why: This is the rule T99's line asks for ('wait on a condition, not a clock'), applied to the window that feature 169's eight jumps were betting on. It stays inside the suite.

decisions.summary: Each next jump waits for four of the timer's logged reads after the last one, so at least one tick falls between two jumps. Pacing ends once the run has started.
decisions.why: A condition replaces a 'sleep 0.15'. It makes the case hold under load, which is what T99 asks.

decisions.summary: Each jump is stamped before it is written, with bash's $EPOCHREALTIME and no fork of date.
decisions.why: This removes the shell lag that caused the red. It is a mechanism inside the asked fix.

decisions.summary: The full wait is pinned by the guard's own 'suspend detected' lines, with jump sizes B x 2^(k-1) decoded to name the latest jump seen. Two checks follow: the run starts at least IDLE_WAIT_S after that jump's stamp, and the timer reads its clock at least 24 times between seeing that jump and the run's start.
decisions.why: This restates case 5's property (a jump restarts the FULL wait) in the timer's own events rather than in slack. It is red first on HEAD under a shell lag and red on a broken guard, as T99's line requires.

decisions.summary: A decode check holds the reading itself: every line on the B grid, the jumps contiguous, and as many lines as the record's suspends. The suite goes from 34 to 37 checks.
decisions.why: Its only job is to make the requested check read the guard's log correctly. That is enforcement of what was asked, not unrequested scope.

decisions.summary: The guard's code is not changed. Only the test file changes.
decisions.why: This is inside the brief, which allowed the guard to change only to expose a timestamp. No timestamp had to be exposed.

decisions.summary: The old 0.35 s slack is retired in favour of IDLE_WAIT_S as a hard floor. The jump size moves from 500 s to B x 2^(k-1) with B = 300 s, checked by arithmetic against IDLE_SUSPEND_S and IDLE_GIVE_UP_S.
decisions.why: These are the test's own GUESS constants, moved to serve the condition-based check. No research claim or map moves.

decisions.summary: The new check pins a full wait after the LAST JUMP THE TIMER LOGGED. It no longer implies that the run began after ALL eight jumps. A timer that detected only its first jump would pass, and the plan says so.
decisions.why: The old implication was a timing assumption: that the shell writes all eight jumps inside one wait. Under a lagging shell a sound timer correctly ends its wait between jumps (the measured 'sleep 1.0 s late' batch), so keeping that implication would keep the very false red T99 removes. The guard's contract (D3: a wall jump past the ticks restarts the wait) is pinned as before, and the plan measured that a non-restarting timer is red in every batch. The undetected-after-first timer is a hypothetical, not a known defect, so nothing defective is left.

decisions.summary: Case 7's upper bound on a condition wait is raised from 8 s to 90 s, after 3 of 64 HEAD copies under load went red. It is fixed in this task.
decisions.why: A found defect (a check refusing good work under load) is fixed as it is found, with the bound case 4b already holds. A green run pays nothing, so this does not narrow what was asked.

decisions.summary: Case 6's 'the losers deferred' went red in 1 of 64 copies at load 133.7. It is not fixed here: it is outside case 5 and its fix is a design choice. It is filed as T104, which lands before T22.
decisions.why: This narrows nothing T99 was asked for, because T99's line is case 5. The defect is not left: it is filed with a reason, a task id and an order, as FR-009 requires, and it lands before T22, the same point T99 lands before.

decisions.summary: The brief cited T76's red as case 5, but it was case 4b, and it was not reproduced in 472 copies. It is filed as T104, which lands before T22.
decisions.why: It is outside case 5, was never reproduced, and is filed with a reason, an id and an order. Nothing in what was asked is dropped.

decisions.summary: The plan labels T99 as not performance work.
decisions.why: This is the conservative direction under FR-013/SC-006: the label can only put T99 behind performance tasks, never ahead of them. It narrows no priority the GM set.

decisions.summary: (waits: <when>) is read only right after the id's bracketed tags, where [perf] is read, so prose quoting the clause waits on nothing
decisions.why: Parsing detail of how a task line states its wait. It narrows nothing asked and stops stray prose from holding a task.

decisions.summary: One wait reading applied in next_independent (free slot), next_performance (task-start's FR-013 picker and the Stop hook's performance-first) and the nothing-running fallback; a waiting performance task no longer triggers FR-013's refusal, its case 'read rather than escaped'
decisions.why: This narrows the accepted FR-013. That spec gives a performance task waiting on another's landing an escape of a recorded reason (FR-012, counted by SC-006), and the plan drops it from the refusal instead. The ruling is against the request ('prioritize performance improvements going forward'; measurement tasks 'counted as a performance task for the purpose of scheduling and coming first'). A performance task that cannot start yet cannot go first, and refusing other work for it idles builders, which defeats the purpose of making everything faster. FR-013's own wording names this exact case as a permitted exception. The reason is still recorded, in git, on the waiting task's committed line, not in the escape log. A startable performance task is refused exactly as before, so the enforcement stays real. Each form is ruled separately in D2a-D2d.

decisions.summary: Form 'T88 lands' / 'T02-T21 land': met when none of the named tasks is open
decisions.why: This is FR-013's named escape case word for word: a performance task waiting on another task's landing. It releases itself when the landing happens, and it is stated on the committed task line.

decisions.summary: T88's 'after T<n>' rule moved from the free slot into the shared reading, so it now also reaches the FR-013 picker and the nothing-running fallback
decisions.why: Same class as D2a: the task cannot start until T<n> is no longer open. Its reach grew to the picker, but its meaning did not change, and it releases itself when T<n> closes.

decisions.summary: Another open line's 'lands before T<n>' holds T<n> (4 open lines in 451 say 'lands before T22')
decisions.why: This is still 'waiting on another task's landing': another task has committed to land first, and 'lands before ...' is the ordering phrase this feature's own FR-009 requires. It is read from prose on a different line, unlike the positional clause, so a passing mention could hold a performance task. It fails toward hiding rather than starting, against the block's stated direction. But the hold ends when that line closes, so it never hides a task for good. Not a defect now: in 451 all 4 measured lines name T22 on purpose.

decisions.summary: Form 'a full day after T.. land(s)': met 24 h past the latest logged landing (land end lines, landed true); T22 a full day after T02-T21 (until 2026-11-22T08:00:27.560Z), T98 a full day after T88 (until 2026-11-22T18:40:27.980Z)
decisions.why: After the landing this is a clock, so it gets D7e's test. Unlike the bare date it is anchored to a logged landing, it has one fixed duration, and it is written on the committed line. A full day's measurement cannot be taken before that day has elapsed (SC-005: 'the first full day after landing'), so the rule is physically impossible to apply sooner, not merely awkward. The GM asked for measurement tasks to count as performance work, and a measurement task taken early measures nothing. T98's stated need is 'a night of rolling dispatch'. The night window cited was 07:50-17:30Z, and the next one after T88's 18:40Z landing is 2026-11-22 07:50-17:30Z. The 24 h hold ends at 18:40Z, about 1h10m after that window closes. So the convention holds T98 only a little longer than its need, and less than the rejected end-of-UTC-day form (00:00Z on 11-23) would. Not a defect.

decisions.summary: Anything else in the parentheses is no wait (fails toward a start the session sees named)
decisions.why: Unreadable text leaves the task inside FR-013's refusal, so this fails toward enforcement, not away from it.

decisions.summary: A bare date is not a form; pinned as no wait
decisions.why: This complies with the earlier plan-review ruling D7e (NOT LEGITIMATE), which this block records. With no form of wait unanchored to a landing, FR-013 is left whole.

decisions.summary: Tasks ticked before the log carried land end lines (451 T02-T05) count as landed long ago
decisions.why: Reads history the log cannot hold. Ticked tasks did land. The latest landing that matters, T11, is logged.

decisions.summary: T22 and T98 lines carry their waits clauses
decisions.why: This is the data the mechanism exists for. Both waits are anchored to logged landings, measured 2026-11-21.

decisions.summary: task_start.rs unchanged; it calls the shared next_performance
decisions.why: Implementation placement. The behavior change is ruled under D2.

decisions.summary: The free slot's PERF_LATER_OK reason now reads 'is started or touches a running task's files'
decisions.why: The message is reworded to match the narrower set of tasks it now covers. Nothing asked is narrowed.

decisions.summary: L7R_WAITS_NOW as the tests' clock seam, else the system clock
decisions.why: Test seam following the L7R_PERMIT_NOW precedent. It acts only on a full-day wait already written on a committed line.

decisions.summary: performance() looks for the heading as text before running its pattern over plan.md
decisions.why: A CPU fix to a cost this change exposed (0.09-0.16 s back to 0.00-0.02 s, measured 2026-11-21). Within the performance work asked for.

decisions.summary: SC-006's count reads off the escape log; a start made while a performance task waits leaves no escape row; left because no SC-006 reader exists
decisions.why: The same narrowing as D2, seen from the spec's side. It is judged fresh, not on the block's appeal to 'T102's plan review notes', which nothing in this bundle backs. Under the defect test only a wrong outcome now is a defect. The block's grep (2026-11-21) finds no reader of 451's SC-006, so nothing misreads today and nothing defective is left. Record for whoever builds that reader or amends the spec: FR-013 and SC-006 still say 'recorded escape', but a waiting task's reason is now on its own line and in the land log, not in the escape log.

decisions.summary: After the date form was dropped, the three tests were rewritten to wait on landings and not rerun red
decisions.why: FR-012's red-first is owed for a refusal that fires, and T102 adds no new refusal: it makes existing ones skip a task that cannot start. The original tests were red on the unchanged hook (357/3, measured 2026-11-21). That the rewritten tests would still be red is argued, not measured: the unchanged hook does not read the clause at all, so its output cannot depend on what the clause says.

decisions.summary: Each of shape's strip patterns (HEREDOC, QUOTED_HEREDOC, UNQUOTED_HEREDOC on '<<', BACKTICK_SPAN on a backtick, INTERPRETER_C on a trimmed text ending in 'c') is searched only where its text holds the literal any match needs, reusing T97's shared::regex::Lazy; cut takes a Lazy.
decisions.why: This is what T103's line asks for (each strip gated on the literal a match needs, as T97 gated the walk's patterns, measured first). It is a [perf] task under FR-013, and the spec's 2026-11-20 request puts performance work first. No answer changes, only the builds.

decisions.summary: QUOTED is replaced by a linear scan (quoted_spans) that reads quoted strings the way the pattern did, with strip_quotes writing from the spans, because the backtracking pattern hung on an unclosed quote followed by many backslashes (corpus rows 3,148 and 7,510 under no_poll_hooks in the background).
decisions.why: A guard that hangs is a defect under constitution XIV's definition (a tool that hangs), and T103 found it in its own file. The fix-as-we-go rule has a known defect fixed before moving on. A pattern replaced by a scan builds no pattern at all, which also serves the line's purpose of no pattern build where none is needed. The differential test (scan equals find_iter on all texts up to 7 characters) is the plan's own evidence that the scan does the pattern's job. No reviewer imposed it as an exactness standard, and it enforces the requested behavior rather than adding scope.

decisions.summary: An arbiter accept clears only the owed/BLOCKED blocks inside the sections of the tasks its trigger names (round trigger #<task>, or the ask subject's task ids via named_tasks), plus their removed blocks; a block outside every named span is not cleared. Scope is read from the trigger, never the question's prose.
decisions.why: A defect fix (fix as we go; constitution XIV's 'a check that passes bad work'): measured 2026-11-21, four accepts cleared 28, 10, 9 and 2 blocks outside the asked task's section, including T76's and T77's unreviewed changes. The rulings themselves scope the accept to the asked task ('This accept stands as the verdict of T79's plan review on the section as it reads now'; T67's and T33's likewise), and FR-043 keeps the verdict per block, so a task round's accept covering only that task's blocks implements what the arbiter ruled and narrows nothing the GM asked.

decisions.summary: An accept whose trigger names no task (5 of 21 accepted plan asks, measured) clears the whole plan as before.
decisions.why: Keeps the existing behavior for asks whose subject was the plan (e.g. ask:420-plan-round3, whose ruling is 'The plan stands as it reads now'); the question was the plan, so the whole plan is its verdict's scope.

decisions.summary: A named task with no section in plan.md or plan-done.md: the whole plan's scope, as plan decided (decision_refusal) reads such a task.
decisions.why: This is the one arm that keeps whole-plan clearing for a named task, and it is not the defect surviving. A task with no section anywhere has no blocks of its own, so its decisions can only be in the plan-stage blocks, and plan decided (decision_refusal) already reads it that way. For such a task the question put to the arbiter was the plan, so the accept's scope matches the question. The over-clearing the section fixes happened only where the named task HAD a section and blocks outside it were cleared too, and D1 ends that.

decisions.summary: A named task whose section is archived (plan-done.md only): nothing recorded, never the whole plan.
decisions.why: FR-044: no review reads plan-done.md and a removed section owes no review, so there is nothing to record; refusing to fall back to the whole plan prevents the over-clearing this task fixes.

decisions.summary: Labeled CONVENTION: the trigger is the scope source because its subject is already a machine-read id (the GM 2026-10-25, the algorithmically easier route where the record is silent).
decisions.why: A mechanism choice inside the fix, applying a standing GM rule; it decides no question the request or rulings settle differently.

decisions.summary: Each named task's tasks.<id> is written CLEAR, declared round-arbiter, at its section digest, with the replaced reviewer entry kept as accepted_over; the tick, push, plan decided and T84's builder-stop guard read that one entry.
decisions.why: Feature 409 (an ask with REVIEW=plan stands as the plan review's verdict) and each cited ruling ('this accept is the plan review's verdict on T67's plan section') require the accept to BE the task verdict; measured 2026-11-21 the store held T33, T46, T67 and T79 BLOCKED though each landed on an accept - a gate reading wrong. Writing it fixes that defect.

decisions.summary: make arbiter-ruled names the scope, each heading recorded CLEAR and the task verdict; a batch's plan accept (BATCH=1) is applied as a single ruling's is.
decisions.why: The output change makes the fix visible where a bare count hid 28 blocks; the batch path recording a plan accept but never applying it is a found defect (observed 2026-11-21 by grep -rn arbiter_accept rust/), fixed here as fix-as-we-go requires.

decisions.summary: The unreviewed changes the over-broad accepts cleared (T56 log path, T77 filing named, T76 make events-refile now takes FROM=) are ruled within and not re-reviewed, T76 being landed and archived.

The section's counts check out (28 = 2 + T76's and T77's 2 + 24 templates; 10 = 2 + 1 + 7; 9 = 2 + 7). On those fragments: T56's log path and T77's naming its filed task are typo-scale. T76's change wires its own tool's FROM= argument into its own make target, which is within its task, narrows nothing and leaves no wrong outcome. T76's section is in plan-done.md, which FR-044 says no review reads.

The cost it states (a file a backgrounded program has not yet written is missed) is a trade-off it names, not a wrong outcome left unfixed.

decisions.id: Performance classification and the n/a rows
decisions.summary: T96 is tagged [perf] as builders'-loop work with no performance checklist (not engine speed), and its step table is n/a (no map).
decisions.why: The GM's 2026-11-21 words ('yes please file that as a performance task'), about the closing checks, and FR-013's definition (the builders' loop) cover the tag. No map changes, so the map rows do not apply.

decisions.summary: Case 4's fixed 1 s sleeps before checks that need an event (the loop's pid file, the hand-started loop's exit, the killed loop's /proc entry, the revived loop's pid) become deadline waits for those events, the checks after them unchanged; R2 added to PIDS for cleanup.
decisions.why: This is exactly the defect T111's line names (a check failing good work under load, constitution XIV). The red-first runs show the old form red and the new form green on a slowed run, start and revive, and the new form still red on a loop that never exits, so the checks keep their job.

decisions.summary: Case 3's fixed 0.5 s sleep before checking the old-form runner becomes a wait until the runner's own argv is in /proc/<pid>/cmdline.
decisions.why: This goes beyond the line's case 4, but it is in the same suite and is the same kind of fix. Under load the check read a pre-exec copy of the suite and passed whatever the hook did, which is a check passing bad work. Fixing a known defect in the file the task owns is within scope and adds no behavior.

decisions.summary: The second prompt's 1 s sleep (line 124) is dropped, not replaced.
decisions.why: Reading the hook's run and judge shows that no sleep could change that check's verdict: a second loop meets the held lock and exits without writing the pid. Removing a wait that does nothing narrows nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: The lock check's message loses 'at once' and becomes 'exits on the lock, where one that took it would loop'.
decisions.why: The words now describe what a deadline wait measures. The hang run shows the check is still red on a loop that never exits, so the check's job is unchanged and only its label moved.

decisions.summary: Each deadline is 300 tries of 0.1 s, labeled a GUESS that only a red run pays.
decisions.why: It is a test-harness bound, not a research constant, and it is labeled GUESS as the project's rules require. A green run pays only its events' latency (measured median 0.027 to 0.200 s, max 0.394 s).

decisions.summary: Eight fixed sleeps in four other hook suites, plus test-finished-run-hooks.sh's settle, wait for an event the next check needs, so a slow host fails good work there too. They are not fixed here: filed as T115, lands before T22.
decisions.why: By the block's own words this is a defect left, so it is ruled, not waved through. Neither the GM's request nor the spec asks for these suites to be fixed. The accepted spec's FR-009, which the session derived from the GM's approval of improvement 4, is the spec's own form for deferring a defect: it needs a why, a filed task id and an order, and the block carries all three (the why, T115, 'lands before T22'). The ruling relies on the second half of the why: each suite owes its own red-first run (FR-012's discipline, as T111's runs here show), which is a separate measured job per suite, not an awkwardness. The first half (the launcher scoped T111 to this suite) is a session's scoping and is given no weight. The purpose of improvement 4 (fewer plan re-rounds through fixing in the task) is not gutted: the defect is filed with a fixed order, not left open-ended.

decisions.summary: Six lines whose checks assert that nothing happened, or whose sleep cannot change the verdict, are listed but not filed: idle-tests 73, 182, 191, 217 and closing-checks 112, 115.
decisions.why: Each line was ruled separately from its text in the block. 73: the timer is alive from its fork, so the check is true whatever the delay. 182: the sleep comes before reading a log that is already fully written, so it cannot change the verdict. 191 and 217: the checks assert no run and no end line; a bounded window is the only form an assertion that nothing happened can take, and the check still catches the behavior on any run where the host is not delayed past the window. 112 and 115: sleeps that order two runs whose checks each read their own run's output, so the order cannot change the verdict. None of the six refuses good work, and none reads the wrong process. Line 104 did read the wrong process: under load it inspected the pre-exec copy of the suite and could pass whatever the hook did. None of the six is a wrong outcome under XIV v2.36.0, so leaving them narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: Three sleeps in idle-tests (96, 210, 211) that sit before a deadline wait are left; they cost only their time.
decisions.why: They fail no good work and pass no bad work. A sleep before a deadline wait is not a defect, and the request does not ask for it to be removed.

decisions.summary: The 'Performance work?' answer is no: this is a test's correctness under load, and the suite's fall from 9.5 s to 2.4 s is a side effect.
decisions.why: This is a scheduling label that narrows no requested work, and the task is being done either way. FR-013's full text was not in the bundle (its index line is cut), so the label was not checked against FR-013's full meaning. None of the GM's words that count a task as performance work (measurement tasks, the closing checks) names this test fix.

decisions.summary: The closing run's make static red (3 tests in guards::event_log_hooks::tests::renumbered in rust/guard/shared) is put down to another builder's uncommitted work that T111 does not touch.
decisions.why: This records the exit evidence and does not narrow the request. The timestamps show the files were written after the run started, and T111 changes no Rust. Whether the landing accepts that is for the land machinery, not a fidelity finding.

decisions.summary: A correction is kept per agent and applied to that agent's later lines; lines filed before it stay as filed, with no general rewrite of the live log.
decisions.why: The spec has no requirement on re-numbered builders; the task exists to stop a re-numbered builder's files being set apart under the old number. In the measured case all three writes came after the SendMessage and the 8 earlier lines wrote nothing, so the forward rule fixes the whole observed wrong outcome. No defect is left: those earlier lines were also re-filed by hand (Found and left). A builder writing before it is corrected was not observed among the 136.

decisions.why: Where the correction is stored is an implementation choice. It narrows nothing that was asked.
